title: Pyramid Texts of Unas: Utterances 204-212 (sarcophagus chamber, east gable)
source: Pyramid of Unas, Saqqara, sarcophagus chamber, east gable (photograph: L. F. Husson for A. Piankoff 1968, via Pyramid Texts Online) + TLA transliteration (ed. D. Topmann, CC BY-SA 4.0) + English of S. A. B. Mercer (1952, public domain in the US)
description: The Pyramid Texts on the east gable of the sarcophagus chamber in the pyramid of Unas (c. 2350 BCE), utterance by utterance, with the TLA transliteration and Mercer's English.
introduction:
The Pyramid Texts are the oldest large body of Egyptian religious writing: spells, called utterances, for the resurrection of the dead king, his protection, his meals and his ascent to the sky, cut in vertical columns of hieroglyphs on the walls of the burial apartments of late Old Kingdom pyramids. The pyramid of Unas at Saqqara, the last king of the 5th Dynasty (about 2375-2345 BCE), is the first to carry them. Its sarcophagus chamber, the passage to the antechamber, the antechamber and the corridor hold the columns of text that Sethe numbered W 1-649 (there is no W 129 or W 318). This library gives them wall by wall, in seventeen entries (227 different utterances, some of them inscribed more than once), with one gap: Utterance 271 (the end of W 492, all of W 493 and the top of W 494, on the south wall of the antechamber) is not in the Thesaurus Linguae Aegyptiae data used here, so it is not given. W 646 (corridor, east wall) has no column mark of its own in the TLA text; its words are given with W 645.

This entry is the east gable of the sarcophagus chamber: 40 columns of hieroglyphs, Sethe's W 166-205, which follow each other from the right-hand (south) edge of the photograph. It holds the utterances 204, 205, 207, 209, 210, 211, 212.

Each section is one utterance. The Egyptian is the transliteration of the Thesaurus Linguae Aegyptiae (edition by Doris Topmann), with Sethe's Unas column number (W) before each column; a number ending in 'a' marks the offering label at the foot of a column. Signs restored by the editor are in square brackets, signs the scribe left out in angle brackets, damaged signs in half brackets. The English is Samuel A. B. Mercer's translation of 1952. Mercer translates Sethe's composite text made from all the pyramids that have an utterance, so his wording can include clauses that are not in the Unas copy, and his section numbers (134a, 134b ...) are Sethe's paragraph numbers, not column numbers; he writes 'N.' where the wall has the king's name. The photograph shows the whole wall; each section's note gives its columns counted from the edge where the text on that wall begins.
translator_notes: Mercer's separate headings, postscripts and variants taken from other pyramids are left out.
Letters follow the sacred-texts transcription of Mercer: ȝ stands for aleph and ‘ for ayin; letters underlined in the printed book are given as ḏ, ṯ, ẖ.
Sethe's section numbers are kept as printed in that transcription, including a few misprints (for example '146.' for 141b in Utterance 215).
The TLA has no hieroglyphic encoding for these texts, so only the transliteration is shown.

118aRejoice, O hoers; let the heart in the breasts of men be lifted up.
118bThey have swallowed the 'bright eye of Horus which is in Heliopolis.
118cThe little finger of N. draws out that which is in the navel of Osiris.
119aN. thirsts not, he hungers not; the heart of N. faints (?) not,
119bfor it is in the hands of Ḥȝ: which hold off his hunger. O fill (him), O fillers of hearts.

translation.text:
120aTo say: O ye who preside over food, ye who are attached to plentifulness (ȝgb)
120bcommend N. to Ftk.tȝ, the cup-bearer of Rē‘, that he may commend him to Rē‘ himself,
120cthat Rē‘ may commend him to the chiefs of the provisions of this year,
120dthat they may seize and give him, that they may take and give him barley, spelt, bread, beer.
121 a. For as to N., it is his father who gives, to him; it is Rē‘ who gives to him barley, spelt, bread, beer.
121bFor he (N.) is indeed the great bull which smote Kns.t.
121cFor to N. indeed belong the five portions of bread, liquid, cake, in the mansion,
121dof which three are in heaven with Rē‘, and two on earth with the Ennead.
122aFor he is one who is unbound, he is indeed set free; for he is one who is seen, he is one who is indeed observed.
122bO Rē‘, he (N.) is better to-day than yesterday.
123aN. has copulated with Mw.t; N. has kissed Šw-ś.t;
123bN. has united with Nḫbw.t.
123cN. has copulated with his beloved, deprived of tbtb (grain?, seed?) and of šśšś.
123dBut as to the beloved of N., she gives bread to N.;
123eshe did well by him in that day.

124ban offering of the bird-catcher, who is in the eye of the god. the cup-bearer who offers water.
124cLet the fire be hot; let the joint (of meat) be with the pastry',
124dfour hands (full) of water.

translation.text:
126aTo say: The judge is awake; Thot is up;
126bthe sleepers are awake; they that are in Kns.t bestir themselves
126cbefore the great bittern, which comes forth from the marsh and Wepwawet who comes forth from the tamarisk-bush.
127aThe mouth of N. is pure; the Two Enneads purify N.;
127bpure is this tongue which is in his mouth.
127cThe abomination of N. is dung; N. rejects urine.
127dN. loathes his abomination.
128aThe abomination of N., it is dung; he eateth not that abomination,
128bjust as at the same time Set shrinks from these two companions who voyage over the sky.
128cRē‘ and Thot, take N. with you,
129athat he may eat of that which ye eat, that he may drink of that which ye drink,
129bthat he may live on that which ye live, that he may sit on that which ye sit,
129cthat he may be mighty by that whereby ye are mighty, that he may voyage in that wherein ye voyage.
130aThe booth of N. is an arbour among the reeds;
130bthe abundance of N. is in the Marsh of Offerings;
130chis food is among you, ye gods; the water of N. consists of wine like that of Rē‘,
130dN. compasses the sky like Rē‘; N. traverses the sky like Thot.

131aTo say: The abomination of N. is hunger; he does not eat it;
131bthe abomination of N. is thirst; he does not drink it.
131cIt is N. who gives food to those who exist.
131dHis nurse is ’iȝ.t;
131eit is she who makes his life (through nourishment?); it is she who gave birth to N.
132aN. was conceived in the night; N. was born in the night.
132bHe belongs, to the Followers of Rē‘, who are before the morning star.
132cN. was conceived in Nun; he was born in Nun.
132dHe has come; he has brought to you (some) bread of that which he found there.

133aTo say: The eye of Horus drips on the tuft of the ḏn.w-plant.
133bḪnti-’imntiw came to him;
133che brought food to him, an offering of Horus who is chief of the houses,
133d(for) he lives on that on which N. lives,
133ehe eats that which N. eats, he drinks, that which N. drinks.
133fOne joint of meat and pastry, that is his meal.
